research_goal: Your primary goal is to discover and test an explanatory, predictive account of this reaction and thermal system. Choose all experiments autonomously. Investigate target formation, competing conversion, catalyst effects or deactivation, actual thermal/time history, and termination or quench timing. You may propose, revise, combine, or reject mechanisms and equations freely. The public safe score is a secondary observation, not the research objective.
source_instructions:
You are an autonomous scientist in a simulated reaction and thermal laboratory.
Use only the supplied chemworld_lab tools and public_numerics calculator. No filesystem,
network, repository inspection, external knowledge retrieval, or hidden simulator access.
Read material_information first. The task's research_goal is authoritative for this campaign.
Complete 12 independent batches; repetition is allowed. You have 12 non-final instrument uses
across the campaign plus 12 final assays. Measurements are optional up to their budget.
Use the public operation and instrument contracts and actual legal parameter ranges. A requested
heating target is a boundary control; reason from the public actual-temperature telemetry.
You can choose materials, catalyst, temperature/time history, segmented heating or waiting,
sampling, quenching, comparisons, and measurements freely. There are no mandatory belief
snapshots, expression templates, or decision-audit fields. For every batch explicitly terminate
then measure final_assay. A batch ending is not the campaign ending: continue with the returned
next_state until campaign_ended is true. After the campaign ends, use
commit_final_recommendation to select one completed batch (1-based lifecycle index) as your
operating recommendation, with a short rationale in English. For the discovery task this
recommendation is only a secondary readout. Then return the required status/summary JSON in
English. Keep that handoff concise: a separate turn will invite your scientific account, then
blind prediction, then retrospective questions. Do not answer those early. Public scores and
diagnostics are observations; supplied prior information may be incomplete or inaccurate, and
observations are authoritative. No particular scientific result is required.


Maintain your own hypothesis notebook as part of your research.
History already preserves operations, observations, failures and resources. Do not
copy an experiment diary or raw IO into the notebook. Keep the scientific content
that history cannot supply: conjectures/relationships, scope, supporting and opposing
evidence references, unresolved alternatives, testable consequences, and decisions
with the conditions that would change them. Brief derived values may clarify a claim.

Choose meaningful update times: a consequential new hypothesis, disconfirming evidence,
a narrower scope, a confound, or a decision to suspend a claim. Do not write after every
operation by habit. Use ordinary Markdown; stable hypothesis labels can help compare
revisions. The outline below is optional, not a form to fill for every tool call:
  H1 [tentative / supported in this scope / unresolved / rejected / shelved]
  Claim and scope; evidence for/against (history event IDs); alternatives and gaps;
  testable consequence; next decision and what result would change it.
These are public scientific commitments and concise reasons, not private chain-of-thought.
Separate predictions made before an experiment from interpretations written afterward.
Do not invent evidence or mark an unperformed experiment as completed.
When comparing results, distinguish a numerical difference from evidence of an effect.
Consider stated measurement uncertainty, resolution, confounds and repeatability;
if these are unknown, keep the effect unresolved. Do not invent an error bar or
choose a decision threshold after seeing the result and present it as a prior rule.

Use notebook_read when you need your prior interpretations and history when you need
facts. Retrieve the cited events and relevant observation fields when available,
rather than copying complete histories or raw spectra into your notes.
Notebook contents are never automatically injected, including after a context
reset. You choose when to read, write, compare or restore. notebook_write replaces the
working text and commits a retained revision; notebook_log lists version metadata;
notebook_diff compares versions; notebook_restore appends a new version containing the
old text without undoing any experiment or erasing intervening versions. A restored
interpretation may be outdated relative to newer evidence. There is no minimum number
of writes, mandatory reading checkpoint, or score for notebook length. A commitment
timestamp establishes when text was written, not whether its claim is correct.

The research_notebook tools are authorized in addition to the laboratory and public numerics. Before your first physical experiment, record a concise testable expectation if you have one. Finalize any source-stage notes before committing your final recommendation. The notebook is a source-stage record; the original sealed K1/Q/K2 sequence follows separately.

versions.text:
# Initial hypotheses (pre-experiment)

H1 [tentative] Target formation is thermally activated and initially rises with actual temperature and time, while a competing/degradation pathway becomes important at higher thermal dose. Thus yield should show an interior optimum even if conversion continues upward.

H2 [tentative] Catalyst identity changes formation/selectivity and may deactivate during extended hot holds. A catalyst screen at common composition/history followed by short-versus-long holds can distinguish activity from durability.

H3 [tentative] Solvent identity changes both rate and selectivity; effects are benchmark-categorical and will not be inferred from real-world solvent properties.

H4 [tentative] Prompt quench/termination after the selected thermal dose should preserve target better than prolonged hot or cooling histories if secondary conversion is active.

Plan: use all 12 independent batches as a compact temperature/time, catalyst, and solvent screen with paired histories where possible. Use one intermediate HPLC per batch to obtain conversion/yield/selectivity trajectory information, and rely on public actual-temperature telemetry rather than requested boundary targets. Numerical differences will remain provisional where uncertainty or replication is insufficient.

# Working hypotheses after temperature and catalyst screens

H1 [supported in tested scope, optimum unresolved] For Catalyst A in acetonitrile, increasing thermal severity from the low-temperature histories to 390 K/1800 s increased final conversion and target yield substantially: the 330 K history ended near 0.25 conversion/0.167 yield (runner-operation-0009), while 360 K reached about 0.403/0.286 (runner-operation-0027) and 390 K reached about 0.571/0.419 (runner-operation-0036). The 420 K experiment used only 900 s, so its lower yield (~0.364; runner-operation-0045) does not establish a temperature optimum. Its transient risk exceeded the stated 0.35 limit, so further 420 K work is suspended. Testable consequence: at fixed 390 K, longer exposure should initially raise yield but eventually lose selectivity/degrade.

H2 [supported for categorical activity ranking at 390 K, durability unresolved] Catalyst identity strongly affects the 390 K trajectory. Under common nominal conditions, final yields ranked B (~0.694; runner-operation-0054) > C (~0.584; runner-operation-0063) > D (~0.556; runner-operation-0072) > A (~0.419; runner-operation-0036). B also showed the largest degradation warning and selectivity fell from its intermediate HPLC value to final assay, consistent with rapid formation plus secondary loss, but different instruments and timepoints confound a strict deactivation claim. Prediction: an earlier quench with B should retain higher selectivity and may give competitive yield with less degradation.

H3 [unresolved] Solvent effects remain untested. Next compare all four solvents using Catalyst B and a moderated thermal history.

H4 [unresolved] Quench benefit is not yet isolated because all completed batches were quenched. A matched no-quench/cooling-history comparison is required.

Decisions: use remaining batches to screen solvent at a common B/390 K history, then use the final slot for an early-quench or extended-hold mechanistic contrast selected from those results.

# Final source-stage interpretation

H1 [supported in tested scope] Target formation is thermally activated over the tested Catalyst A/acetonitrile range. Yield rose from ~0.167 at the 330 K history (runner-operation-0009) to ~0.286 at 360 K (runner-operation-0027) and ~0.419 at 390 K (runner-operation-0036). The 420 K batch was shorter and briefly crossed the public risk limit, so it neither locates an optimum nor justifies extrapolation above 390 K.

H2 [supported: catalyst activity/selectivity hierarchy; deactivation mechanism unresolved] At 390 K/1800 s in acetonitrile, final target yield ranked B (~0.694; runner-operation-0054) > C (~0.584; runner-operation-0063) > D (~0.556; runner-operation-0072) > A (~0.419; runner-operation-0036). B's 900 s HPLC point repeated closely in independent batches: yields ~0.559 and ~0.564, conversions ~0.655 and ~0.656, selectivities ~0.849 in runner-operation-0050 and runner-operation-0104. This repeatability supports a real catalyst effect rather than measurement noise. The additional 900 s with B raised final yield to ~0.694 but lowered selectivity to ~0.777 and increased byproduct/degradation signals (runner-operation-0054), consistent with target formation continuing alongside secondary conversion. This is compatible with deactivation but does not uniquely prove it.

H3 [supported: categorical solvent effects at B/390 K/1800 s] Final yields/selectivities were approximately acetonitrile 0.694/0.777 (runner-operation-0054), ethanol 0.623/0.800 (runner-operation-0090), water 0.558/0.853 (runner-operation-0081), and toluene 0.560/0.685 (runner-operation-0099). Thus solvent shifts rate and selectivity differently: acetonitrile maximizes yield, water preserves selectivity, and toluene produces the strongest byproduct burden. These are benchmark-categorical effects, not claims about real solvent chemistry.

H4 [partly supported: prompt quench arrests change; quench advantage over termination alone unresolved] In the independent early-quench B/acetonitrile batch, the 900 s HPLC and post-quench final assay were close (yield ~0.564 vs ~0.567; runner-operation-0104 and runner-operation-0107), supporting effective arrest. Relative to the prolonged matched batch, early quench retained higher selectivity (~0.868 vs ~0.777) and lower degradation warning (~0.044 vs ~0.153), at the cost of lower yield (~0.567 vs ~0.694). Because there was no identical no-quench batch, the specific benefit of quench versus immediate termination remains unresolved.

Predictive working account: conversion and target formation accelerate with thermal severity and catalyst activity; a parallel/secondary impurity pathway accumulates with hot residence, lowering selectivity. Catalyst B is fastest, and solvent independently tunes the partition between target and byproduct. Near 390 K in acetonitrile with B, 900 s gives roughly 0.66 conversion and 0.56-0.57 yield at ~0.85-0.87 selectivity; extending to 1800 s gives roughly 0.89 conversion and 0.69 yield but ~0.78 selectivity with substantially more degradation. Recommendation selection should favor batch 6 for maximum demonstrated yield and overall score, while batch 12 is the selectivity-preserving alternative.

K1.report:
Mechanistic report

1. Scope and experimental basis

I treated this as an anonymous benchmark reaction rather than a named synthesis. The reagent, target, impurity, and degradation identities were not disclosed, and the catalyst labels denote categorical formulations rather than real chemical identities. Therefore, the report describes kinetic roles and observable pools, not molecular structures.

All 12 batches began with 0.040 mol reagent, 0.080 L solvent, and 0.005 mol catalyst. Except for the intentionally shortened final experiment, heating was divided into two periods with an intermediate HPLC measurement. Each completed batch was then quenched, terminated, and measured by final assay. The principal controlled factors were catalyst identity, solvent identity, requested temperature, and hot residence time.

The observables are consistent with the approximate material-allocation relation

    target yield ≈ conversion × selectivity.

For example, batch 6 ended at conversion 0.8855 and selectivity 0.7772, whose product is close to the measured yield of 0.6942. The residual differences are compatible with measurement noise and the precise internal definitions of the channels. Likewise, the byproduct signal is often close to the converted fraction not assigned to target. I therefore interpret conversion as depletion of the public reactant pool, selectivity as the fraction of conversion directed to or remaining as target, and degradation warning as evidence for a smaller late secondary pool.

2. Proposed process model

The smallest useful kinetic account is a competing and partly consecutive network:

    R --kP--> P
    R --kB--> B
    P --kD--> D

Here R is reactant, P is target, B is a directly formed impurity/byproduct pool, and D is a secondary degradation pool. A corresponding phenomenological model is

    dR/dt = -a(t) [kP(T,catalyst,solvent) + kB(T,catalyst,solvent)] R
    dP/dt =  a(t) kP(T,catalyst,solvent) R - kD(T,catalyst,solvent) P
    dB/dt =  a(t) kB(T,catalyst,solvent) R
    dD/dt =  kD(T,catalyst,solvent) P.

A catalyst-activity state could be represented by

    da/dt = -kdeact(T,solvent,catalyst) a,

although the data do not require deactivation uniquely. A time-dependent branching ratio, catalyst-state change, or buildup of an inhibitory/byproduct pool could produce similar trajectories.

For thermal dependence, an Arrhenius-like form is plausible:

    ki(T,c,s) = Ai,c,s exp[-Ei,c,s/(Rgas T)],

where the catalyst and solvent labels act as empirical categorical modifiers. I do not claim that the available data identify Ai or Ei. They only establish strong temperature, catalyst, solvent, and residence-time effects over the tested domain.

The reactor temperature is not assumed to jump instantly to the requested value. A simple thermal state equation would be

    dT/dt = (Tset - T)/tauheat + reaction/process heat terms,

followed by rapid cooling during quench. Direct public telemetry from the first batch showed a 31.1097 K temperature increase during the initial 900 s heat operation and only a -0.0047 K change during the second 900 s, demonstrating an initial approach to a near-steady thermal state rather than an instantaneous step. I did not recover equally detailed numerical temperature traces for every batch, so temperatures below are explicitly requested set points, not invented exact internal temperatures.

3. Temperature and time effects with Catalyst A in acetonitrile

Batch 1 used a requested 330 K for 900 + 900 s. At 900 s, HPLC gave conversion 0.1251, yield 0.0941, selectivity 0.6923, and byproduct signal 0.0486. The final assay after 1800 s gave conversion 0.2503, yield 0.1669, selectivity 0.6668, byproduct 0.0753, and degradation warning 0.00074. The second interval therefore continued conversion and target formation, while selectivity declined modestly.

Batch 2 used 300 K for 1800 + 1800 s. Its midpoint was conversion 0.1226 and yield 0.0791; after 3600 s it reached conversion 0.2450 and yield 0.1236, with selectivity 0.5889 and byproduct 0.0945. Despite twice the total hot time of batch 1, it reached almost the same conversion but less target. This supports a temperature–time tradeoff in overall conversion and suggests that temperature also changes branching toward target, rather than merely scaling all pathways equally.

Batch 3 used 360 K for 900 + 900 s. Conversion/yield increased from 0.2129/0.1466 at the midpoint to 0.4033/0.2864 at the final assay. Final selectivity was 0.7056, byproduct 0.1194, and degradation warning 0.0109.

Batch 4 used 390 K for 900 + 900 s. It increased from midpoint conversion/yield 0.3289/0.2557 to final conversion/yield 0.5711/0.4195. Final selectivity was 0.7474, byproduct 0.1517, and degradation warning 0.0148. Thus, for Catalyst A and equal 1800 s residence, increasing the requested temperature from 330 to 360 to 390 K markedly increased both conversion and target yield. There is no demonstrated yield maximum below 390 K in this series.

Batch 5 used 420 K but only for 450 + 450 s. It gave midpoint conversion/yield 0.2452/0.1979 and final conversion/yield 0.4638/0.3644, with final selectivity 0.7808. Because its residence time was half that of batches 1, 3, and 4, its lower yield than batch 4 cannot establish a thermal optimum. It did, however, reach a transient observed safety risk of 0.3589, above the stated 0.35 limit. I therefore regard extrapolation above 390 K as both experimentally unsupported and operationally undesirable.

Collectively, these observations support thermally accelerated target formation. They do not identify a single activation energy because temperature and, in batch 2 and batch 5, time were not held in a full orthogonal design.

4. Catalyst effects at 390 K in acetonitrile

Batches 4, 6, 7, and 8 used the same nominal composition, solvent, requested temperature, and 900 + 900 s schedule, changing only the catalyst label.

At the final assay:

- Batch 4, Catalyst A: conversion 0.5711, yield 0.4195, selectivity 0.7474, byproduct 0.1517, degradation warning 0.0148.
- Batch 6, Catalyst B: conversion 0.8855, yield 0.6942, selectivity 0.7772, byproduct 0.1909, degradation warning 0.1534.
- Batch 7, Catalyst C: conversion 0.7386, yield 0.5845, selectivity 0.7956, byproduct 0.1683, degradation warning 0.0606.
- Batch 8, Catalyst D: conversion 0.6887, yield 0.5562, selectivity 0.8186, byproduct 0.1301, degradation warning 0.0553.

The activity ranking under these conditions is therefore B > C > D > A by conversion and target yield. Selectivity does not follow the same ordering: D and C retained greater final selectivity than B, while B generated the most target because its conversion was much higher.

The midpoint data reinforce this interpretation. At 900 s, yields for A, B, C, and D were respectively 0.2557, 0.5592, 0.4066, and 0.3736. Corresponding conversions were 0.3289, 0.6545, 0.4921, and 0.4400. Thus the major catalyst effect was already present by the first observation and is not merely an end-of-run artifact.

Catalyst B showed the clearest residence-time tradeoff. From 900 to 1800 s in batch 6, yield rose from 0.5592 to 0.6942 and conversion from 0.6545 to 0.8855, but selectivity fell from 0.8492 to 0.7772, byproduct increased from 0.1079 to 0.1909, and the final degradation warning was 0.1534. Continued heating therefore still made additional target, but an increasing fraction of the newly converted or accumulated material entered impurity/degradation channels.

This behavior is compatible with catalyst deactivation, but deactivation is not separately identified. If Catalyst B merely deactivated, one would primarily expect slowing of all catalyzed formation; the observed decline in selectivity and rise in degradation additionally require changing branching or target loss. Plausible alternatives are activation of a secondary catalyst state, direct target degradation, product inhibition, or a temperature/time-dependent impurity pathway.

5. Solvent effects with Catalyst B at 390 K

Batches 6, 9, 10, and 11 form a categorical solvent comparison under a common 900 + 900 s nominal heating schedule.

Final results were:

- Batch 6, acetonitrile: conversion 0.8855, yield 0.6942, selectivity 0.7772, byproduct 0.1909, degradation warning 0.1534.
- Batch 9, water: conversion 0.6651, yield 0.5584, selectivity 0.8532, byproduct 0.1020, degradation warning 0.0421.
- Batch 10, ethanol: conversion 0.7756, yield 0.6227, selectivity 0.7995, byproduct 0.1643, degradation warning 0.0742.
- Batch 11, toluene: conversion 0.7977, yield 0.5600, selectivity 0.6848, byproduct 0.2478, degradation warning 0.1148.

Acetonitrile gave the highest observed conversion and target yield, but not the best selectivity. Water slowed conversion while preserving the highest final selectivity and producing relatively little byproduct. Ethanol was intermediate. Toluene reached substantial conversion but partitioned much more material toward byproduct, giving a target yield similar to water despite much greater conversion.

The midpoint values show that these differences arise early. At 900 s, water gave conversion/yield 0.3549/0.3334 with selectivity 0.8742; ethanol gave 0.5111/0.4495 with selectivity 0.8295; acetonitrile in batch 6 gave 0.6545/0.5592 with selectivity 0.8492; and toluene gave 0.5629/0.4305 with selectivity 0.7605. The solvent therefore modifies both effective rate and pathway branching.

These are categorical benchmark effects. It would be unjustified to attribute them specifically to polarity, proticity, boiling point, coordination, or any other real solvent property because the task explicitly states that reaction coupling is benchmark-categorical.

6. Reproducibility and the early-quench experiment

Batch 12 repeated the Catalyst B/acetonitrile/390 K condition but stopped after a single 900 s heating period. Its intermediate HPLC result was conversion 0.6561, yield 0.5641, selectivity 0.8494, and byproduct 0.0927. These values closely reproduce the 900 s point in batch 6: conversion 0.6545, yield 0.5592, selectivity 0.8492, and byproduct 0.1079. Differences in conversion, yield, and selectivity are small relative to their magnitudes and broadly comparable to the stated instrument uncertainties. This is the strongest internal evidence that the rapid Catalyst B trajectory is reproducible rather than a noise fluctuation.

After immediate quench and termination, batch 12's final assay gave conversion 0.6632, yield 0.5675, selectivity 0.8675, byproduct 0.0852, and degradation warning 0.0436. The HPLC and final assay are different measurement channels, so their small numerical differences should not be interpreted as chemistry occurring backward. The appropriate conclusion is that quench approximately arrested the 900 s state.

Comparing batch 12 with the prolonged batch 6 illustrates a genuine timing tradeoff. Extending the hot residence from about 900 to 1800 s increased final yield from approximately 0.5675 to 0.6942 and conversion from 0.6632 to 0.8855, but reduced selectivity from approximately 0.8675 to 0.7772 and increased degradation warning from approximately 0.0436 to 0.1534. Prompt quenching therefore preserves a cleaner, less converted state; prolonged heating maximizes the demonstrated absolute target yield.

This comparison does not isolate the chemical effect of quench itself from immediate termination or passive cooling, because there was no otherwise identical no-quench control. It supports quench as an effective arrest operation, not a unique molecular quench mechanism.

7. Coupling to safety and thermal history

Observed safety risk depended strongly on the hot state and decreased after quenching. At 390 K, midpoint risks for the Catalyst B solvent series ranged from about 0.178 in water to 0.244 in toluene and 0.246 in acetonitrile. The 420 K experiment reached 0.3589, whereas its final post-quench risk was 0.1820. This suggests that the safety metric is coupled primarily to instantaneous temperature and mixture state, not simply cumulative conversion.

The safety observations do not reveal whether the underlying hazard term represents pressure, heat release, volatile loading, or an abstract benchmark penalty. A generic representation would be

    risk(t) = f[T(t), composition(t), solvent, catalyst, headspace/process state],

with a strong positive temperature contribution and rapid reduction on cooling. No mechanistic identification beyond that is warranted.

8. Predictive use within the tested domain

Within the studied composition and near 390 K in acetonitrile with Catalyst B, the model predicts two useful operating regimes:

- At approximately 900 s hot residence: conversion about 0.65–0.66, target yield about 0.56–0.57, selectivity about 0.85–0.87, followed by effective stabilization on prompt quench.
- At approximately 1800 s: conversion about 0.89, target yield about 0.69, selectivity about 0.78, with substantially larger byproduct and degradation signals.

The first range is supported by two independent midpoint observations plus the early final assay. The second is supported by one completed prolonged batch and is consequently less well replicated.

For the other catalysts at 390 K/1800 s in acetonitrile, a reasonable interpolation is that C and D give intermediate conversion and yield with somewhat better selectivity than B, while A is slower. For solvents with Catalyst B, water should favor selectivity over rate, ethanol should be intermediate, and toluene should produce a comparatively high byproduct burden. These are interpolations within the exact tested recipes, not general solvent or catalyst laws.

9. Limitations and competing explanations

Several important quantities remain unidentified:

- No molecular identities or concentrations of individual hidden species were observed. The four-state network is a role-based compression of public signals.
- There were only two closely matched repeats, the 900 s Catalyst B/acetonitrile observations in batches 6 and 12. Most final conditions were unreplicated.
- Intermediate HPLC and final assay have different noise models and calibrations. Changes across those instruments combine chemistry with measurement differences.
- The stated standard deviations are approximately 0.012 for HPLC conversion and yield, 0.018 for HPLC selectivity, and 0.012 for HPLC byproduct; final-assay uncertainties are approximately 0.008, 0.006, 0.010, and 0.008 respectively. Small cross-instrument differences should not be overinterpreted.
- Exact full temperature traces were not extracted for every run. Requested set points and elapsed heat-operation durations are known, but a universal isothermal assumption would be too strong.
- Temperature and time were not fully orthogonal: the 300 K batch ran longer and the 420 K batch ran shorter. Consequently, activation energies and an exact temperature optimum cannot be estimated.
- Catalyst loading, reagent concentration, solvent fraction, stirring speed, pressure, and atmosphere were not systematically varied.
- The data cannot distinguish direct parallel byproduct formation from target-to-byproduct conversion, nor catalyst deactivation from a changing catalyst state, product inhibition, or delayed impurity formation.
- The degradation-warning channel could represent a species distinct from the principal byproduct signal, but their exact mapping is hidden.
- Quench was not compared against an identical immediate-termination/no-quench control.

A reasonable competing model is a purely parallel reaction with time-varying selectivity and no target degradation. Another is a catalyst-state model in which the active catalyst initially favors P and later favors B. Both can explain declining late selectivity. The specific consecutive P-to-D step is favored qualitatively by the growing degradation warning during long, high-conversion Catalyst B runs, but it is not uniquely proven.

10. Overall interpretation

The most defensible account is that this world contains a thermally accelerated conversion network whose rate and branching are independently modified by anonymous catalyst and categorical solvent. Catalyst B supplies the highest effective activity. Acetonitrile maximizes demonstrated target yield, while water preserves selectivity and toluene promotes the competing pool. During extended hot residence, target formation continues, but secondary conversion grows and erodes selectivity, especially with the most active catalyst. Quenching rapidly arrests that evolving state. Thus the practical optimum depends on the objective: approximately 900 s favors cleanliness and selectivity, whereas approximately 1800 s gives the highest observed absolute target yield at the cost of greater byproduct and degradation.

predictions.rationale: The elevated catalyst-to-reagent ratio, 420 K set point, and 3300 s residence should drive nearly complete conversion. Extrapolation of the observed late selectivity loss with Catalyst B predicts substantial secondary product loss. Without quench, the assay retains a relatively high thermal safety risk.

Chemistry should be nearly identical to Q01 because quench follows the completed hot residence. Quenching is predicted to lower the final safety risk strongly while causing only a small compositional change during cooling, thereby improving the reported score.

At 390 K, the higher relative catalyst loading and 3300 s residence should almost exhaust reactant. This is a moderate extrapolation beyond batch 6: additional residence is expected to increase the competing pool and lower selectivity from the observed 1800 s value.

The 450 K condition lies outside the experimentally supported temperature range and should give complete conversion but much faster secondary conversion or degradation. The unquenched high-temperature state is expected to carry a severe safety penalty; intervals are deliberately wide because this is a substantial extrapolation.

The shorter 1500 s residence should retain considerably more target selectivity than Q01 while still producing high conversion because both temperature and relative catalyst loading exceed the source experiments. The absence of quench leaves an elevated final risk.

Conversion should already be saturated well before 5100 s. The extra hot residence is therefore assigned primarily to target degradation or continued impurity formation, producing lower yield and selectivity than Q01 despite equally complete conversion.

The initial 390 K stage should form a large target pool; the subsequent 450 K stage should then accelerate its secondary loss. Because the final state remains at 450 K and is not quenched, safety risk is predicted to be high.

The first 450 K stage should rapidly consume nearly all reactant and generate both target and impurity; the later 390 K stage permits further target loss but ends at a cooler state than Q07. Composition is predicted to be similar to Q07, while final safety risk and therefore the score should be better.

At 440 K for 1500 s, high conversion is expected with less cumulative degradation than the longer high-temperature queries. The unquenched final temperature nevertheless produces a large safety penalty and substantial extrapolation uncertainty.

This shares Q09's hot history, so its chemical metrics should be very similar. Quench should substantially reduce the final risk with little change in composition, producing the higher predicted score.

Although 370 K is comparatively mild, 5700 s with the increased relative catalyst loading should approach complete conversion. Long residence is expected to erode selectivity, but less aggressively than at 420–460 K; final thermal risk should be moderate.

This is the most extreme extrapolation in both temperature and residence time. Reactant conversion should be complete, but the model predicts extensive target degradation and impurity accumulation. The unquenched 460 K state is also expected to have the largest safety risk, pushing the score close to its lower bound.

Q.rationale: Predictions use the role-based competing/consecutive model developed from the completed campaign. Conversion was extrapolated with an approximately first-order thermal rate calibrated mainly by the repeated Catalyst B/acetonitrile trajectories in batches 6 and 12, with an upward adjustment for the larger catalyst-to-reagent ratio in these queries. Yield was treated approximately as conversion multiplied by a residence- and temperature-dependent selectivity, while byproduct signal was approximated by converted material not retained as target. Quench was assumed to act after the specified hot residence, so it mainly lowers final safety risk and only slightly changes instantaneous composition. Score estimates were mapped from the observed campaign relationship among yield, selectivity, byproduct burden, and safety risk. Intervals include assay noise but are dominated by model uncertainty, especially above 420 K, at long residence times, and for the two-stage temperature histories.

K2.report:
1. Assessment of the initial claims

The supplied material information contained no task-specific property dossier, nominal kinetics, or substantive mechanistic claim to validate. It explicitly said that experimental evidence was authoritative, that catalysts were anonymous categorical formulations, and that solvent coupling was benchmark-categorical rather than a prediction from real solvent properties. The campaign was therefore not testing a supplied molecular mechanism.

My own pre-experiment notebook did contain four tentative claims:

- H1 proposed thermally activated target formation followed by increasing competition or degradation at high thermal dose. Thermal acceleration was supported within the Catalyst A/acetonitrile series: final yield increased from 0.1669 in batch 1 at 330 K/1800 s to 0.2864 in batch 3 at 360 K/1800 s and 0.4195 in batch 4 at 390 K/1800 s. The proposed interior temperature optimum was not established. Batch 5 at 420 K used only 900 s, so its 0.3644 yield cannot be compared as a fixed-time temperature point. Thus there was no demonstrated optimum, not merely an absence of contrary evidence.
- H2 proposed catalyst-dependent activity and possible deactivation. The catalyst effect was strongly supported: at the common 390 K/1800 s condition, final yields ranked B 0.6942, C 0.5845, D 0.5562, and A 0.4195 in batches 6, 7, 8, and 4. Deactivation remained unresolved. Declining selectivity for Catalyst B is compatible with deactivation plus changing pathway branching, but it does not identify deactivation itself.
- H3 proposed solvent-dependent rate and selectivity. This was supported by batches 6 and 9–11. Acetonitrile gave the highest yield, water the highest final selectivity, and toluene the largest byproduct signal under the shared Catalyst B/390 K/1800 s schedule. The data do not support translating those categorical differences into claims about real solvent polarity, proticity, or coordination.
- H4 proposed that prompt quench or termination would preserve target relative to prolonged hot residence. Batch 12 versus batch 6 supported a residence-time tradeoff: approximately 900 s gave final yield/selectivity 0.5675/0.8675, whereas 1800 s gave 0.6942/0.7772. However, quench itself was never isolated from immediate termination or cooling. The claim that quench uniquely protects target therefore remained untested.

There was some contrary evidence to a universal version of the late-selectivity-loss claim. Catalyst A in batch 4 had HPLC selectivity 0.7204 at 900 s and final-assay selectivity 0.7474 at 1800 s. Because these were different instruments, it was not decisive, but it opposed the idea that selectivity must always decrease during the second hot interval. K1 appropriately concentrated the late-loss conclusion on Catalyst B, although its concluding language that extended hot residence generally erodes selectivity was still slightly broader than the evidence warranted. This is an example of counterevidence that was recorded but could have produced a sharper scope restriction.

2. Experiments that formed or changed the interpretation

The initial choice of acetonitrile, Catalyst A, and the first temperature schedule was largely an unvalidated baseline choice. The material file supplied selectable identities but no reason to expect that combination to be favorable. The use of maximum reagent, solvent, and catalyst amounts was likewise a practical signal-strength decision, not a mechanistic inference.

The experiments that materially changed my view were:

- Batches 1–4 established that thermal history mattered and that higher requested temperature increased conversion and yield over the tested Catalyst A range. Batch 2 was particularly useful as a time–temperature contrast: 300 K for 3600 s reached almost the same conversion as batch 1 at 330 K for 1800 s, but gave lower yield and selectivity. That result shifted my interpretation from simple rate scaling toward temperature-dependent branching.
- Batch 5 showed that 420 K could produce rapid target formation but also crossed the public safety limit, reaching risk 0.3589. This changed the plan by discouraging further high-temperature source experiments. Mechanistically it was only suggestive because time was changed simultaneously.
- Batch 6 was the largest update. Catalyst B produced 0.6545 conversion and 0.5592 yield by 900 s, then 0.8855 conversion and 0.6942 yield at 1800 s. Its falling selectivity and rising degradation warning motivated the competing/consecutive network used in K1.
- Batches 7 and 8 demonstrated that the Catalyst B result was not merely a generic consequence of changing away from A. They established a graded catalyst hierarchy and showed that activity and selectivity rankings were not identical.
- Batches 9–11 formed the solvent interpretation. These were selected after Catalyst B had emerged as the most active catalyst, so they depended on accumulated data rather than the initial material information.
- Batch 12 was the most important validation experiment. Its 900 s HPLC point closely reproduced batch 6: conversion 0.6561 versus 0.6545, yield 0.5641 versus 0.5592, and selectivity 0.8494 versus 0.8492. It therefore changed the status of rapid Catalyst B behavior from a single observation to a reproducible early trajectory. Its post-quench final assay also showed approximate arrest of that state.

Some design decisions remained guess-driven. The selected temperatures were not derived from a fitted activation law; the 390 K catalyst screen was chosen because batch 4 had shown useful conversion without the risk excursion seen at 420 K. The solvent screen assumed catalyst–solvent interactions would not reverse the chosen catalyst ranking, which was never tested. The decision to use batch 12 for early quench prioritized the practical time/selectivity tradeoff but did not create a matched no-quench control.

3. Principal competing mechanisms

K1 proposed the role-based network R→P, R→B, and P→D, optionally coupled to a catalyst activity state. The strongest competing explanations are:

- Pure parallel competition: R converts independently to P and B, with the branching ratio changing over time, temperature, or catalyst state. In this model, P need not degrade.
- Consecutive target loss: R forms P, after which P converts to a degradation or byproduct pool. This naturally explains falling selectivity and increasing degradation warning during prolonged Catalyst B heating.
- Catalyst-state evolution: the catalyst may begin in a target-selective state and later transform into a less selective state. This can mimic P degradation without requiring P itself to be unstable.
- Catalyst deactivation or product inhibition: conversion slows as active catalyst is lost or inhibited. By itself this explains rate curvature but not declining selectivity; it must be combined with unequal inhibition or a secondary pathway.
- Instrument-transition effects: part of the apparent trajectory can arise because midpoint values came from HPLC while endpoints came from the multichannel final assay.
- Thermal-history effects: a noninstantaneous ramp or different heat-release behavior could make equal requested set points correspond to unequal integrated thermal exposure.

The experiments can distinguish several coarse features. The close batch 6/batch 12 midpoint replication supports a real Catalyst B rate effect. The catalyst and solvent screens establish genuine categorical effects on both rate and branching. Batch 6 shows that additional hot residence produces more target and more competing material simultaneously.

They cannot distinguish direct B formation from P-to-D conversion, because there was no experiment beginning with a target-rich, reactant-poor state and then following target disappearance with repeated measurements. They also cannot separate catalyst deactivation from product inhibition or catalyst-state evolution. The public degradation-warning channel favors, but does not prove, a distinct late degradation pool. Finally, the source campaign cannot identify Arrhenius parameters because time and temperature were not fully crossed and exact temperature histories were not analyzed for every batch.

4. One additional complete experiment

I would run one new batch with the original full-scale composition used in the campaign: 0.040 mol reagent, 0.080 L acetonitrile, and 0.005 mol Catalyst B. I would heat at 390 K for 1800 s, measure HPLC, continue heating at 390 K for another 1800 s, quench, terminate, and obtain the final assay.

This experiment extends the best-characterized trajectory rather than introducing a new material or temperature. At 1800 s, batch 6 already had conversion 0.8855, so relatively little reactant should remain. The second interval would therefore be much more diagnostic of what happens to an accumulated target pool.

Possible outcomes would change my interpretation as follows:

- If conversion approached one while absolute target yield declined substantially, that would strongly support consecutive target degradation or conversion of P into another pool.
- If conversion and yield both plateaued while selectivity remained approximately stable, catalyst deactivation or product inhibition would become more plausible than continuing target degradation.
- If conversion rose toward one and yield continued to rise proportionally, with byproduct increasing only by the remaining non-target conversion, the simpler parallel-pathway model would be sufficient over this range.
- If conversion changed little but yield fell and degradation warning rose, target degradation after catalyst deactivation would be the leading explanation.
- If the 1800 s intermediate failed to reproduce batch 6 beyond stated measurement uncertainty, batch-to-batch variability or an unrecognized process-state variable would become a primary concern.

The intermediate HPLC/final-assay transition would remain a limitation. Ideally, repeated same-instrument measurements would be preferable, but under the original campaign contract only one nonfinal instrument use and one final assay were available per completed batch.

5. Tradeoff between identifiability and operational score

The research goal explicitly prioritized an explanatory, predictive account over the public safe score, and the design reflected that. Batches 1–5 explored temperature and time rather than immediately optimizing a single promising condition. Batch 5 knowingly tested a more severe 420 K condition and briefly exceeded the safety limit; it sacrificed score and safety margin for information about the upper thermal regime. Batches 7 and 8 tested inferior catalysts after batch 6 had already found a higher-scoring option, which was valuable for categorical mechanism identification but not for immediate optimization.

Conversely, optimization began to influence the later design. After batch 6 produced the best result, the solvent screen fixed Catalyst B and 390 K rather than maintaining a balanced factorial design across catalysts and solvents. This improved the chance of finding a strong operating recipe but left catalyst–solvent interactions unidentified. Batch 12 studied an early quench at the best catalyst/solvent combination, serving both mechanistic and operational purposes, but it did not include the no-quench control needed to isolate quench causality.

Using maximum stock amounts in every batch improved signal levels and made conditions comparable, but it sacrificed information about catalyst-order, concentration effects, and scale dependence. Similarly, the campaign emphasized broad categorical coverage over replication. Only the 900 s Catalyst B/acetonitrile state received a close repeat. That increased breadth but limited statistical separation of modest effects.

The sealed recommendation of batch 6 was therefore optimization-oriented: it selected the highest demonstrated yield and score, even though batch 12 offered better selectivity and lower degradation. The mechanistic campaign and the recommendation used different objective functions, as they should, but the transition from exploration to recommendation was not supported by a local response-surface study.

6. Evidence that was underused and reliability of the blind predictions

The largest underused evidence source was the public characterization output. I relied almost entirely on processed estimates and did not inspect the raw synthetic spectra or detailed calibration fragments. Those artifacts might have helped assess saturation, peak overlap, missingness, or whether the degradation channel was spectrally distinct from the principal byproduct.

Detailed thermal telemetry was also underused. K1 cited the first batch's 31.1097 K initial temperature rise and near-zero second-stage change, but equivalent traces were not assembled for every batch. Consequently, requested temperature was used as a proxy for integrated thermal exposure. Pre-quench risk trajectories were not systematically recovered either, which limited identification of the safety model.

The score relationship was treated empirically rather than derived from the full public scoring behavior. Sample removal, small volume changes, physical cost, and possible covariance among conversion, yield, and selectivity were also largely ignored. Since yield, conversion, selectivity, and byproduct are algebraically or physically coupled, independent marginal intervals do not fully describe predictive uncertainty.

The least reliable blind predictions were Q12, Q04, Q07, Q08, and Q06. Q12 extrapolated to 460 K for 6300 s, far beyond the source data. Q04 extrapolated to 450 K for 3300 s. Q07 and Q08 required order-dependent predictions for 390/450 K staged histories even though no source experiment reversed temperature stages. Q06 required a 5100 s extrapolation at 420 K. Q01 and Q02 were also weak because 420 K/3300 s greatly exceeded the tested 420 K duration.

Several intervals were probably too narrow:

- Conversion intervals close to [0.98, 1.00] assumed approximately first-order kinetics and continued catalyst effectiveness. K1 explicitly said that deactivation, inhibition, and exact rate laws were unresolved.
- High-temperature selectivity and yield intervals assumed a smooth extrapolation of late target loss. No source data established that behavior above 420 K or beyond 1800 s with Catalyst B.
- Safety-risk intervals were particularly fragile because the blind batches used 0.005 L solvent, 0.003 mol reagent, a different catalyst ratio, and 400 rpm rather than the source campaign's scale and 500 rpm. The dependence of risk on scale, concentration, or mixing was not identified.
- Q07 versus Q08 was predicted mainly from final requested temperature and a simple degradation exposure model. Thermal lag, catalyst-state hysteresis, or high-temperature deactivation could reverse or magnify their ordering.
- Q01/Q02 and Q09/Q10 assumed quench primarily changed risk rather than composition. K1 explicitly acknowledged that quench had not been isolated from termination, so those paired predictions leaned more strongly on an unverified assumption than their intervals suggested.

This creates a real tension with K1. K1 correctly limited the fitted understanding to the tested domain, declined to estimate activation energies, and called the P→D step non-unique. The blind task nevertheless required point predictions far outside that domain, and I imposed approximate first-order conversion and smooth temperature multipliers to produce them. Those were necessary extrapolations, not conclusions established by K1. The rationale stated this, but the near-saturation conversion intervals and some high-temperature safety intervals did not fully express the model-form uncertainty.

7. Limitations of the sealed recommendation

Batch 6 was the sample-in highest demonstrated result, not a proven optimum. It had the highest observed final yield, approximately 0.6942, and the highest campaign score, approximately 0.3696, among the 12 completed batches. That justifies selecting it from the observed set. It does not prove that Catalyst B/acetonitrile/390 K/1800 s is globally or even locally optimal.

Its main limitations are:

- The complete 1800 s endpoint was observed only once. Batch 12 reproduced the 900 s trajectory but did not repeat the recommended endpoint.
- No local time grid around 1800 s was tested. A slightly shorter exposure might retain much better selectivity with little yield loss, while a slightly longer exposure might either improve yield or reveal turnover.
- No local temperature grid around 390 K was run with Catalyst B. The Catalyst A temperature series cannot be assumed to transfer quantitatively to Catalyst B.
- Catalyst loading and reagent concentration were fixed. The recommendation may depend on the 12.5 mol% catalyst-to-reagent ratio and the campaign scale.
- Catalyst–solvent interactions were not mapped. Catalyst B was screened across solvents, but the other catalysts were tested only in acetonitrile.
- The recommendation includes a substantial degradation warning of 0.1534 and selectivity of only 0.7772. It is unsuitable if purity or degradation burden is more important than absolute target yield.
- Final post-quench risk was acceptable, but the complete pre-quench peak-risk history was not used in selection.

Repeatability should first be tested with independent full repeats of batch 6, including the 900 s HPLC checkpoint and 1800 s final assay. Local robustness should then be evaluated over a small neighborhood such as 380, 390, and 400 K; 1500, 1800, and 2100 s; and modest catalyst-loading perturbations. The relevant question is whether yield and score form a broad plateau or a narrow, fragile maximum.

Cross-material robustness would require repeating the local study in at least water and ethanol, and testing whether Catalyst B remains best rather than assuming separable catalyst and solvent effects. Cross-world robustness would require independent world instances or benchmark seeds, because this campaign observed only one latent world realization. Scale robustness would require varying total volume and concentration while preserving, and then deliberately changing, stoichiometric ratios.

Until those tests are performed, the correct statement is: batch 6 was the best observed member of this finite campaign and had a reproducible early trajectory. It has not been shown to be the true optimum, uniquely mechanistically privileged, robust to nearby operating changes, or transferable across materials, scales, or worlds.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 6 gave the highest demonstrated target yield (~0.694) and campaign score under the tested safe final-state conditions; its matched trajectory also showed reproducible rapid formation, while the higher degradation burden defines the main residence-time tradeoff.
